blocks.text: There, however, instead of There is none whom the warm or the charming poets call, some read, not badly, There is none whom Tityus, etc. If this reading is accepted, Petronius would be speaking not of Prometheus but of Tityus, of whom the greatest poet says in book 6 of the Aeneid:
— and a monstrous vulture with hooked beak, pecking at the immortal liver. — —
And long before, the father of fables, Odyss. λ' [l]:
Γῦπε δέ μιν ἑκάτερθε παρημένῳ ἧπαρ ἔκειρον, Δέρτρον ἔσω δύνοντες, [Gype de min hekaterthe parēmenō hēpar ekeiron, Dertron esō dynontes,]

And two vultures, perched on either side, were digging into his liver, having pierced the skin within. Perhaps, then, a corrupt reading of Petronius' words deceived Fulgentius. But consider the passage of Valerius Flaccus on the Promethean herb, Argonautica book 2, line 357:

[III, 69] — it brings forth the Caucasian flower from the blood of the Promethean flesh, herbage nourished by the thunder, which that sacred gore, amid the snows and the grim frosts, hardens and puts forth, when the vulture, its gullet sated, rises from the crags and sprinkles it from its open beak.
If, I say, you compare this passage of Valerius with these lines of Apollonius on this same herb, Argonautica book 3, line 850:

Πρωτοφυὲς τό γ᾽ ἀνέσχε καταστάξαντος ἔραζε Αἰετοῦ ὠμηστέω κνημοῖς ἐνὶ Καυκασίοισιν, Αἱματόεντ᾽ ἰχῶρα Προμηθῆος μογεροῖο. [Prōtophyes to g' aneschе katastaxantos eraze Aietou ōmēsteō knēmois eni Kaukasioisin, Haimatoent' ichōra Promēthēos mogeroio.]

you will plainly see that Valerius has made a vulture out of the eagle, just as among our own writers Theophylact does when he wants the eagles of which Christ speaks in Matth. XXIV, 28. to be taken as vultures. Ἐπὶ νεκρὸν σῶμα, he says, συνάγονται ὀξέως οἱ ἀετοὶ, οἱ γῦπες δηλαδή [Epi nekron sōma … synagontai oxeōs hoi aetoi, hoi gypes dēladē]. To a corpse the eagles, that is, the vultures, quickly gather. Gesner [col. 315] also observes that Albertus and certain other more recent writers often confuse the vulture with the eagle. And Albertus defends himself with the authority of Aristotle, who, he writes, assigns the eagle and the vulture to the same genus; this Gesner rightly denies. Yet Albertus had a reason for believing it. For he had read neither the Greek text of Aristotle nor a Latin version made from the Greek text, but one made from the Arabic. Such were the times in which Albertus lived. Then there was no one among the Latins who read the Greek writers in Greek or rendered them into Latin: only the Arabs were consulted, who had translated into their own language whatever existed in Greek, and from their versions barbarous translators rendered the Greek works into Latin after a fashion. The Arabs, moreover, extend the word نسر [nasr] neser, which properly means eagle, even to the vulture. Hence they sometimes ascribe to the neser things that are proper to the vulture. Thus what Alkazuinius says belongs to the vulture: النسر يتبع العساكر لطعمه في لحم القتال [al-nasr yatbaʿu al-ʿasākir li-ṭuʿmihi fī laḥm al-qitāl] that the neser follows armies, in order to feed on the flesh of the slain. Likewise, ياكل الجيف حتي لا يقدر علي الطيران [yākulu al-jiyaf ḥattā lā yaqdiru ʿalā al-ṭayarān] that it gorges itself on carcasses so much that it can no longer fly. But these words of Damir too, in the chapter نسر [nasr] Neser, are proper to the vulture rather than to the eagle: وهو حاد البصر يري الجيفة من اربع ماية فرسخ وكذلك حاسة شمه الي النهايه لكنه اذا شم الطيب مات لوقت [wa-huwa ḥādd al-baṣar yarā al-jīfa min arbaʿ māya farsakh wa-kadhālika ḥāssat shammihi ilā al-nihāya lākinnahu idhā shamma al-ṭīb māta li-waqtihi] It has very keen sight, so that it sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. Its sense of smell is likewise extremely intense. Accordingly, when it smells perfume, it dies on the instant. For in sight the [III, 70] eagle is indeed strongest, as was proven in its place ^{c)}; but the power of smell is believed to be greater in the vulture. Hence Lucretius, book 4:
Though bees are drawn from far by the scent of honey, and vultures by carcasses. — —

And Apuleius in the first Apology: But if he has caught with his nostrils the smell of home cooking, he surpasses dogs and vultures in keenness of scent. For to what dog, to what vulture would anything of the Alexandrian sky be perceptible as far away as the borders of the Aeenses? And Sidonius, book 7, letter 14: They display subtlety of smell, as if the vulture did not excel in scent. Hence the verse in common use:
The vulture excels in smell, the spider in touch.
